title.narrative: ET: Combined Efforts Against CSEC in Amhara Region (GAA)

description.narrative:
The project is part of the Girls Advocacy Alliance program - a lobby and advocacy program which aims to achieve the goals: 1) girls and young women in Ethiopia become less vulnerable to FGM, child marriage, trafficking and sexual exploitation of children; and 2) girls and young women in Ethiopia actively participate in meaningful economic activities. This project specifically focuses on the themes/issues: commercial, sexual exploitation of children and economic exclusion of girls and young women.
The L&A activities planned in the project will target a wide range of actors including CSOs, communities, government and private sector representatives. The project will be implemented in Amhara Region of Ethiopia through Jerusalem Children and Community Development organization (JeCCDO) - a local, child-focused NGO operating in the country.

condition.narrative:
Context analysis from parent activity: The second most populous country in Africa, Ethiopia’s population was estimated to be 90 million by end of 2015. The population is young with 45% of the total population being children less than 15 years of age, while only 3.2% is estimated to be over age 65. Ethiopia’s society is patriarchal that holds the rights of women and children in a lower regard, and is also deeply religious where the role of religion in the lives of the people is significant. Ethiopia is a low-income country with a gross national income (GNI) of USD 330 per capita (2009), which has grown at an average rate of 8% per annum since 2005. The vast majority of Ethiopia’s population (85%) depends on agriculture for a living. Women constitute 49.5 % of the total population and contribute to over 65% of agricultural production, storage and processing. The 2011 EDHS shows that 38 % of Ethiopian women are currently employed compared to 80% of men. In addition, women are highly represented in the informal sector, representing more than 60% of the informal work force. The majority of women entrepreneurs are in micro-enterprises (65%) and many of them lack business development skills for improved competitiveness and management. Women tend to assume most of domestic work: 59 % of female participants in the 2011 EDHS survey said that their husbands rarely participate in doing household chores. Women own only 19 % of the land (CSA 2007/2008). The country has three levels of federalist system of government, comprising the federal government; nine administrative regions and two chartered city administrations; and over 800 woredas (districts) and sub-cities.
Domestic child trafficking is predisposing girls into commercial sex work. Commercial sexual exploitation of children is prevalent in most urban areas in Ethiopia like the city of Bahir Dar. According to a study by FSCE, 64% of the child sex workers interviewed in Bahir Dar had tried out life as domestic servants before moving into the business of prostitution. Research also indicates that over a quarter of nearly 50,000 women and children involved in commercial sex work in Ethiopia are victims of trafficking. The push factors for both internal and cross border trafficking and unsafe migration are poverty, family conflict, family (parental) deaths, peer pressure, early marriages and other harmful practices, socio-economic factors such as overpopulation, scarce resources, lack of employment opportunities, and limited access to social services.
Most are losing faith in the education system and prefer to opt for migration and drop out of school as the education system fails to guarantee them job opportunities. In 2010, 49% of children aged 15 and 16 years were out-of-school (almost 2 million - 53% girls). In 2008/09 girls comprised 27.6% of the total number of students enrolled in grades 11 and 12 (preparatory grades), 46.2% in technical and vocational training and 29% in higher education in 2007/08. Girls between the age group of 10 to 17 are the most affected by school drop-out. These groups are also more at risk of being trafficked, forced into commercial sex. Parents and families put pressure on their young children, especially girls to migrate and send remittances to support the families.
The review of relevant laws and policies in Ethiopia provides a general picture that the present legal and policy framework, despite minor flaws, provides acceptable protection to children and women from sexual violence. But implementation of existing laws, policies, strategies and plans is weak, and cultural traditions and attitudes of the community hinder the enforcement of the laws. Besides, the current CSO legislation restricts local and international NGOs from advocating on rights related issues, and available policies and plans fail to adequately address the problem of commercial sexual exploitation of children.

Risk analysis from parent activity: 1. Political/Legal: a. The Charities and Societies organizations regulation may have an influence on the application on implementation of selected strategies to advocate and lobby. The existing CSO regulations and directives may slow implementation of the planned lobby and advocacy activities targeting the Charities and Associations Agency (ChSA). To mitigate this risk JeCCDO will:
i. Network with similar Civil society organization ii. Properly learn emerging dynamics in the sector and align programs with the New CSO legislation iii. Work with CSOs which have better leverage to influence the government such as Women Associations, Youth Associations. 2. Resource: a. partner staff turnover . b. Inflation: Materials price may rise and budget assigned may fail to fully address costs. • In order to mitigate both staff turnover and inflation, JeCCDO will develop staff retention mechanism and immediate replacement in time of resignation. Also strengthening documentation and make smooth transition could be solution. With regards to inflation, timely procurement and activity execution as well as looking for additional fund will be our mitigation strategy. 3. Program Implementation: a. Limited interest of civil society organization to join interventions that focus on advocacy and lobby. In order to increase interest from CSO’s JeCCDO will design and apply innovative and appealing advocacy and lobbying strategy. Also making the responsible government offices to take the lead in the process will be given priority. b. Staff turn- over and continuous reshuffling at the government offices where we work with. It can be mitigated through maintaining principle/agreement based working relationship and establishing Memorandum of Understanding on the planned strategies/interventions c. The practice of collaboration and working in partnership among CSO actors may not go as efficiently as expected. In order to reduce this risk, JeCCDO will: i. Clarify roles, and regularly revise them ii. Increase communication and learning with partners and stakeholders that take part in joint actions iii. Create platforms that ease sharing of learning and best practices among partners iv. Capacity building training on partnership management/partnering skills for partners d. Community elders may be reluctant to include children in decision making processes because of culture Mitigation: continuous awareness raising to on the importance of involving children in decision making and as agents of change e. Child victims of CSEC may lack the courage to publicly speak about CSEC for lobby and advocacy purpose Mitigation: use of anonymous recordings, quotations, etc
